title: What is disaster recovery on AWS: the four strategies from cheapest to fastest: Backup & Restore (hours to recover), Pilot Light (keep minimum resources running, scale up on disaster), Warm Standby (scaled-down copy always running), Multi-Site Active-Active (full copy in another region, instant failover): and what is RPO (how much data you can lose) vs RTO (how long you can be down)?
shortTitle: Disaster Recovery on AWS: Four Strategies, RPO and RTO
keyPoints: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window before the disaster.
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long you can afford to be down before recovery is complete.
Backup and Restore is cheapest but slowest: RPO equals backup frequency, RTO is hours while you rebuild from scratch.
Pilot Light keeps the critical core (replicated database) always running; RPO is small, RTO is shorter because only the app tier starts.
Warm Standby runs a scaled-down fully functional copy; RPO is small, RTO is minutes because the system is already running.
Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in multiple Regions with near-zero RPO and RTO, at the highest cost and complexity.
Choose per workload based on business criticality, and test failover regularly because untested DR plans fail when needed.

s1_definition.oneliner: DR runs from cheap-and-slow to costly-and-instant -- Backup and Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site Active-Active -- and you pick based on RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long you can be down).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** – how much data you can afford to lose, measured as a time window; tighter RPO requires more frequent or continuous replication.
- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** – how long you can afford to be down; tighter RTO requires more standby infrastructure ready to take over.
- **Backup and Restore** – keep backups, rebuild on disaster; RPO = backup frequency, RTO = hours.
- **Pilot Light** – keep the critical core (replicated DB) always running; scale up the app on disaster; RPO = seconds to minutes, RTO = tens of minutes.
- **Warm Standby** – run a scaled-down fully functional copy; scale up on disaster; RPO = small, RTO = minutes.
- **Multi-Site Active-Active** – full capacity in multiple Regions serving live traffic; RPO and RTO near zero.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must survive its main building being destroyed. Backup and Restore is keeping copies of all records in a warehouse and rebuilding from scratch -- cheap but takes hours. Pilot Light is keeping just the vault mirrored in a second building, lights off, ready to furnish quickly. Warm Standby is a smaller working branch that you scale up rapidly. Multi-Site Active-Active is two full branches both serving customers, so if one is destroyed the other keeps going.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Disaster recovery on AWS is how I restore a workload after a failure large enough to take out the primary environment, and there are four strategies that trade cost against recovery speed. I choose between them using RPO (how much data I can lose) and RTO (how long I can be down). Tighter objectives always cost more.

From cheapest to fastest: Backup and Restore keeps backups and rebuilds from scratch on disaster with hours of RTO. Pilot Light keeps the critical core running (a replicated database) and starts the app on disaster. Warm Standby runs a scaled-down fully functional copy that scales up in minutes. Multi-Site Active-Active runs full capacity in multiple Regions with near-zero RPO and RTO at the highest cost.

The senior point is that you pick per workload, not one strategy for the whole organization, and a DR plan is worthless unless you test the failover regularly. Untested recovery fails exactly when needed.

At National Bank of India the core payment ledger needed near-zero RPO and RTO, so it ran Active-Active across two Regions. The customer API used Warm Standby with a thirty-minute RTO. Internal reporting stayed on Backup and Restore. We ran quarterly game-day failover drills to prove the targets were real.

Remember one sentence: choose a DR strategy per workload based on RPO and RTO, from Backup and Restore (cheap, hours) to Active-Active (expensive, near-instant), and test the failover regularly because untested plans fail when needed.
